passages.title: Five oaths and the certain punishment
passages.tafsir:
Surah At-Tur opens the way a witness opens testimony: with a solemn oath. In ayat 1–6 Allah swears by five things He has made — a mountain, a written Book, a House in the heavens, a raised roof, and a sea — and in ayat 7–8 He states the thing sworn to: **the punishment of your Lord is certainly coming, and nothing can push it back.**

That is the unity of the passage. Everything in ayat 1–6 exists to carry the weight of the two short lines that follow. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: Allah swears by His creation, a testimony to His great ability, that His torment will surely befall His enemies, and they will have no way of escaping it.

## The shape that holds it together

Arabic oath-speech has two halves. The first is the swearing itself — here the ayat beginning "By…". The second is what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the *jawāb al-qasam*: "the fact for which the oath is sworn," the statement the oath was made in order to establish. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies the halves exactly: ayat 1–6 constitute the swearing of an oath, and ayah 7 is its answer — assuring that the torment of Allah will come to pass, and none will be able to avert it.

So while you recite ayat 1–6 you are held in suspense. Majestic realities are named one after another with no completed sentence — and then ayah 7 lands: **إِنَّ عَذَابَ رَبِّكَ لَوَاقِعٌ**, "Verily, the torment of your Lord will surely come to pass." Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah "contains the subject of the vow."

## Ayah 1 — the mountain that has trees

**وَٱلطُّورِ** — "By Mount Ṭūr."

Ibn Kathir gives a piece of vocabulary most readers never learn: *aṭ-Ṭūr* is a mount that **has trees**. A mountain with no trees is called *jabal*, not *ṭūr*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same, adding that the word *Ṭūr* in Hebrew means a mountain that has trees.

Which mountain? Ibn Kathir says aṭ-Ṭūr is the mount that has trees, similar to the mount where Allah spoke to Mūsā while Mūsā was upon it, and the mount on which Allah began the prophethood of ʿĪsā. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies it here as Mount Sinai, situated in the land of Madyan, where the Prophet Mūsā (peace be upon him) had the honour of Allah speaking to him. Qurṭubī is cited there for a further report: that there are four mountains of Paradise in this world, and Ṭūr is one of them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws out why the oath matters beyond honouring the mountain. Swearing an oath by Ṭūr carries a special significance and honour for the mount — but it also signifies that certain injunctions have been revealed by Allah for people to follow, and that compliance with them is obligatory. The oath, in other words, is not only a mark of honour. It carries an obligation.

## Ayat 2–3 — the Book written on an open scroll

**وَكِتَٰبٖ مَّسۡطُورٖ ۝ فِي رَقّٖ مَّنشُورٖ**

These two ayat are one oath: a Book *masṭūr* — "the Book inscribed," as Ibn Kathir renders it — and then ayah 3 tells you what it is written on. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *raqq* means fine parchment, a fine piece of skin used for the purpose of writing on it, and so it is usually translated simply as paper. The whole phrase is rendered there as "a book, written on an unrolled scroll" — Ibn Kathir has "in parchment unrolled." A scroll rolled up keeps its contents to itself; a scroll unrolled is a document held open in front of you.

What is the Book? The sources give several answers and do not force a choice:

- **Al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ,** the Preserved Tablet — one view reported by Ibn Kathir.
- **The divinely revealed inscribed Books that people recite** — also reported by Ibn Kathir, who notes this is why Allah adds "in parchment unrolled."
- **A person's own account-book of deeds** — cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Qurṭubī.
- **The Qur'an itself** — the view of some of the scholars, also cited there from Qurṭubī.

Held together, these are not really in competition. Every one of them is a *writing that will be produced as evidence*: what was decreed, what was revealed, or what you did. In a passage whose whole subject is a punishment that cannot be averted, an oath sworn by an open written record is quietly terrifying. Nothing is improvised on that Day; it is already written, and the page is already open.

## Ayah 4 — the House that is never empty

**وَٱلۡبَيۡتِ ٱلۡمَعۡمُورِ** — "And by Al-Bayt Al-Maʿmūr," the Populated House.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr is the Kaʿbah in the heaven, meant for the angels' service, parallel to the Kaʿbah on earth. Ibn Kathir reports from the Two Sahihs, in the hadith about al-Isrā', that after the Prophet ﷺ ascended to the seventh heaven he said: "Then, I was taken to Al-Bayt Al-Maʿmūr. It is visited every day by seventy thousand angels who will not come back to visit it again." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same report from Sahihain and explains the last clause: because every day *other, new* angels take their turn to visit it.

Sit with that number. Seventy thousand angels a day, not one of them a repeat visitor — an unbroken tide of worship. Ibn Kathir explains that the angels worship Allah there and perform ṭawāf around it just as the people of the earth perform ṭawāf around the Kaʿbah; Al-Bayt Al-Maʿmūr is the Kaʿbah of those who reside in the seventh heaven, standing parallel to the Kaʿbah on earth. He adds that every heaven has its own house of worship, which is also the direction of prayer for its residents, and that the house located in the lower heaven is called Bayt al-ʿIzzah — "and Allah knows best."

One detail in both commentaries is worth pausing over. During the Isrā' journey the Prophet ﷺ saw Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl (peace be upon him) reclining with his back against Al-Bayt Al-Maʿmūr. It was Ibrāhīm who built the Kaʿbah on earth — and, as Ibn Kathir says, surely the reward is compatible with the action. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out the same way: because he built Allah's House below, Allah has blessed him with a special connection with Al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr above.

## Ayah 5 — the roof raised high

**وَٱلسَّقۡفِ ٱلۡمَرۡفُوعِ** — "And by the roof raised high."

Ibn Kathir reports through Sufyān ath-Thawrī, Shuʿbah and Abū al-Aḥwaṣ — all from Simāk, from Khālid bin ʿArʿarah — that ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib said this means **the heaven**. Sufyān adds that ʿAlī then recited: "And We have made the heaven a roof, safe and well-guarded. Yet they turn away from its signs" (21:32). Similar was said by Mujāhid, Qatādah, as-Suddī, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Jarīr preferred it.

The image is domestic and enormous at once. A roof is what stands over you while you sleep — the thing you never look at because it is simply always there. And the ayah ʿAlī reached for ends in exactly that reproach: the heaven is guarded, it is full of signs, "yet they turn away from its signs." Ayah 5 asks you to look up at a ceiling you long ago stopped noticing.

## Ayah 6 — the sea

**وَٱلۡبَحۡرِ ٱلۡمَسۡجُورِ** — "And by the sea that is Masjūr."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *masjūr* is a passive participle derived from *sajr*, a word used in several different senses. Two readings run through the sources, and both are held by major authorities:

**1. The sea kindled with fire.** One of the senses of *sajr* is to kindle with fire, and some of the commentators take the participle that way here: the oath is by the sea *as it will be* on the Day of Resurrection, kindled with fire and become a raging fire surrounding the people in the plain of gathering. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel ayah "And when the seas become as blazing fire" (81:6), and reports this from Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib from ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib, and likewise from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Mujāhid, ʿAbdullāh bin ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an exchange reported by Qurṭubī: a Jewish man asked ʿAlī, "Where is Hell?" He replied, "The sea" — and the man, a scholar of the previous scriptures, confirmed it.

**2. The filled sea.** Qatādah said *masjūr* means the "filled sea." Ibn Jarīr preferred this, with a simple argument Ibn Kathir records: "The sea is not lit with fire now, so it is filled." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this is the interpretation adopted by Maulānā Ashraf Thānawī.

Ibn Kathir also notes that the majority say the oath refers to the oceans of the earth. Where the scholars differ like this, the honest thing is to hold both readings: an ocean brimming today, an ocean that may burn tomorrow — and either way, something utterly beyond your control being called to witness.

## Ayat 7–8 — the answer to the oath

**إِنَّ عَذَابَ رَبِّكَ لَوَٰقِعٞ ۝ مَّا لَهُۥ مِن دَافِعٞ**

"Verily, the torment of your Lord will surely come to pass. There is none that can avert it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same two lines: "The punishment of your Lord is sure to fall. There is nothing to push it back."

This is the answer the five oaths were sworn to establish. Ibn Kathir says ayah 7 contains the subject of the vow, indicating that His torment will surely strike the disbelievers.

Then ayah 8 closes the last door. Ibn Kathir's gloss is exactly that: when Allah decides to send the torment upon them, none can prevent it or stop it from striking them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same of the pair — the torment of Allah will come to pass, and none will be able to avert it.

## What these ayat did to the people who first heard them

The sources preserve three moments, and they are the best commentary on the passage.

**A man converted by two lines.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Qurṭubī that Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, before embracing Islam, once went to the holy city of Madīnah to negotiate regarding the prisoners of the battle of Badr. When he arrived, the Prophet ﷺ was reciting Sūrah aṭ-Ṭūr in the Maghrib prayer, and his voice could be heard outside the mosque. When he reached ayat 7 and 8 — "The punishment of your Lord is sure to fall. There is nothing to push it back" — he suddenly felt that his heart would burst through fear, and felt at that moment that he would not be able to move unless the torment descended on him. He embraced Islam instantly. Ibn Kathir records Jubayr's testimony about that same recitation from the Two Sahihs, through a chain of narration that includes Mālik: "I heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting Sūrat aṭ-Ṭūr while praying Maghrib. Surely, I have never heard a more beautiful voice or recitation than his recitation."

**A caliph laid low.** Ibn Kathir cites al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr Ibn Abī ad-Dunyā, from Jaʿfar bin Zayd al-ʿAbdī: one night in al-Madīnah, ʿUmar went out investigating the welfare of the Muslims and passed by the house of a man who was standing in voluntary prayer. ʿUmar stood quietly, listening; the man was reciting Sūrat aṭ-Ṭūr, until he reached "Verily, the torment of your Lord will surely come to pass. There is none that can avert it." ʿUmar said: "**By the Lord of the Kaʿbah, this is a true vow.**" He dismounted his donkey and sat next to a wall for a while, then went back to his house and fell ill for a month. During his illness the people would visit him, not knowing what caused it. May Allah be pleased with him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the same incident with ʿUmar reciting the sūrah himself, heaving a cool sigh when he came to these verses, and remaining ill for about twenty days.

**A woman doing ṭawāf.** Al-Bukhārī recorded that Umm Salamah complained of being ill to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "Perform ṭawāf of the Kaʿbah behind the crowd, while you are riding." She said: "So I performed ṭawāf while the Messenger of Allah was praying beside the House, reciting aṭ-Ṭūr." That is where this sūrah lived in the Prophet's ﷺ own practice — recited in Maghrib, recited beside the Kaʿbah.

## Living it

Ayat 1–6 are, in the end, an instruction in where to look: at a mountain where Allah spoke to a prophet, at an open written record, at a House kept full by worshippers, at the sky over your head, at the sea. Ayat 7–8 tell you what that looking is for. The witnesses are all things you cannot argue with and cannot move; the verdict they attest to is of the same kind.

ʿUmar's response is the model — and notice what it was not. He did not debate the ayah, and he did not shrug at it. He affirmed it — "this is a true vow" — and it entered him so deeply that he was ill for weeks. Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim heard it once, before he was a Muslim, and embraced Islam on the spot. This passage was never meant to be information. It is a summons, and the answer those two men gave is the one it is asking for.

passages.title: The Day of shaking and the deniers' rebuke
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat are the answer to a question the surah has just raised. In ayat 7–8 Allah swore by His creation that **"the torment of your Lord will surely come to pass. There is none that can avert it."** Ibn Kathir explains that the first of these is the subject of the vow — His torment will surely strike the disbelievers — and the second means that when Allah decides to send that torment, none can prevent it or stop it from striking them.

The natural question is: *when, and to whom?* Ayah 9 begins with the words **"On the Day…"** — and everything from here to ayah 16 is that Day, unrolled: first the sky and the mountains coming apart, then the people who laughed at the warning being driven into the Fire, and finally the words spoken to them once they arrive. The passage moves from cosmic scale to a face-to-face rebuke, and it never once loosens its grip.

## The oath that made ʿUmar ill

Before the description begins, it is worth feeling the weight of the oath it hangs on. Ibn Kathir relates that al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Ibn Abi ad-Dunya recorded that Jaʿfar bin Zayd al-ʿAbdi said: one night in Madinah, ʿUmar went out investigating the welfare of the Muslims and passed by the house of a man who was standing in voluntary prayer. ʿUmar stood quietly, listening to his recitation. The man was reciting Surat at-Tur, until he reached *"Verily, the torment of your Lord will surely come to pass. There is none that can avert it."* ʿUmar said, **"By the Lord of the Kaʿbah, this is a true vow."** He dismounted his donkey and sat next to a wall for a while, then went back to his house and fell ill for a month. During his illness people would visit him, not knowing what had caused it. May Allah be pleased with ʿUmar.

That is the response of a man who heard the words as news rather than as decoration. The ayat that follow are simply the details of what ʿUmar had already accepted.

## Ayah 9: what *mawr* actually does

**يَوْمَ تَمُورُ السَّمَاءُ مَوْرًا** — rendered "on the Day the heavens will be shaken violently," and in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "the Day when the sky will tremble, a horrible trembling."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the lexical sense of *mawr* is violent shaking, or movement caused by unrest — not orderly motion, but the motion of something disturbed. The early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir each reach for a different edge of the word:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah:** "Shaking violently."
- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (in another report): "Split."
- **Mujahid:** "Spin violently."
- **Ad-Dahhak:** "The earth will violently spin and move by the command of Allah, and its areas will violently move towards each other."

Ibn Jarir preferred this last explanation, and Ibn Kathir gives his reason: because of the meaning of the word *mawr*, which denotes meanings of spinning and shaking at once. So the reports gather around a single picture — not something that merely trembles, but something wrenched out of its settled order: shaking, splitting, spinning, its parts driven violently against one another.

## Ayah 10: the mountains

**وَتَسِيرُ الْجِبَالُ سَيْرًا** — the mountains will *move*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is that they "will fade away and become scattered particles of dust blown away by the wind."

Put ayat 9 and 10 side by side and you have the two things a human being instinctively treats as fixed: the sky overhead and the mountains underfoot. On that Day the one above is shaken out of its order, and the ones below are scattered as dust on the wind. Nothing in the created world is offered here as a place to stand.

## Ayah 11: woe — and to exactly whom

**فَوَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلْمُكَذِّبِينَ** — *"Then woe that Day to those who denied."* Ibn Kathir: woe to them that Day as a result of Allah's torment, punishment and affliction that He will direct at them.

The word chosen is **al-mukadhdhibīn** — not "the ignorant," not "the sinners," but *the deniers*: those who were told, and answered, "That is a lie." The whole passage is built around this one act. It returns in ayah 14 — *"This is the Fire which you used to deny"* — as the reason they are there. Denial is not treated as an intellectual position that happened to be mistaken; it is treated as the thing they will be shown, and made to stand in front of.

## Ayah 12: the diagnosis — falsehood and play

**الَّذِينَ هُمْ فِي خَوْضٍ يَلْعَبُونَ** — *"those who were, in their falsehood, playing,"* rendered elsewhere as "those who amuse themselves with falsehood." Ibn Kathir's explanation is exact: **they live in this life in falsehood, and make the religion the subject of their mockery and jest.**

This is the most searching ayah of the eight, because it names an attitude rather than a doctrine. Ibn Kathir does not describe solemn opponents of the truth; he describes people for whom the religion has become material for mockery and jest — a topic to be batted around, not a claim to be weighed. And notice that in his wording this is not an episode but the shape of a whole life: *they live in this life in falsehood.*

The structure of the passage is itself an argument. A man who treats the warning as a game has already assumed the warning is not real. Ayat 9 and 10 have just told him what is real. Ayah 12 therefore lands as the exposure of a wager badly made.

## Ayah 13: the game ends

**يَوْمَ يُدَعُّونَ إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا** — *"The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the Fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing."* Ibn Kathir glosses **yudaʿʿūn** as: they will be violently driven and shoved. He then records that Mujahid, ash-Shaʿbi, Muhammad bin Kaʿb, ad-Dahhak, as-Suddi and ath-Thawri all explained the ayah the same way: **"They will be violently shoved into the Fire."**

The reversal here is the point. In ayah 12 they were the ones playing, in charge of the game, deciding what to make light of. In ayah 13 they are the ones acted upon — *driven and shoved*, in Ibn Kathir's words — handled without dignity, moved by a force they have no say in. The one who would not walk to the truth is carried to the consequence. And the ayah's own wording will not let it pass as a gentle summons: they are pushed down by force, *with a horrible, forceful pushing*.

## Ayat 14–16: four doors, all closed

The last three ayat are speech — and Ibn Kathir identifies the speakers: **the angels of punishment will say these words to them, while admonishing and chastising them.** Read them as four attempts to escape, each shut in turn.

**1. "It was never real."** *"This is the Fire which you used to deny."* The denial is not argued with; it is simply set beside the thing denied. Nothing more needs saying.

**2. "It's some kind of trick."** *"Is this magic, or do you not see?"* (ayah 15). Ibn Kathir has already told us the register of these words — admonishment and chastisement, not inquiry. Two options are put to them and both are absurd where they now stand: is what is in front of you sorcery — or are your eyes simply not working?

**3. "I can hold out."** *"Enter therein"* — Ibn Kathir: enter the Fire, *which will encircle you from every direction* — *"and whether you are patient of it or impatient of it, it is all the same."* Ibn Kathir gives the sense as: whether you endure its torment and afflictions or not, you will never avert it or be saved from it. This is a devastating line, because endurance is the one strategy a human being always has left: bear it, and eventually it passes. Here that lever is disconnected. Ibn Kathir's wording leaves no gap in it — *never* avert it, *never* be saved from it.

**4. "This is excessive."** *"You are only being requited for what you used to do."* Ibn Kathir closes: **surely, Allah is never unjust with anyone; most certainly, Allah recompenses each according to their deeds.** The whole terrifying scene turns out to be, precisely, justice. What they meet is their own record.

## Living it

Because ayah 12 diagnoses a posture rather than a creed, this passage has something to say to a believer who has never denied anything.

- **Take the news as news.** ʿUmar heard *"the torment of your Lord will surely come to pass"* and was ill for a month. That is what it looks like when the words are received rather than merely recited.
- **Watch what you make light of.** The people of ayah 12 are described not as arguing against the religion but as making it, in Ibn Kathir's words, the subject of their mockery and jest. That habit is available to anyone, in any age.
- **Do not lean on the fixed things.** Sky and mountain are this passage's own examples of permanence, and both are undone by ayah 10. Whatever you have quietly decided is too solid to fail belongs on that list.
- **Know when endurance still counts.** Ayah 16 shows endurance that changes nothing, because the torment there can never be averted. The warning, though, arrives now — while there is still something to be done with it.

## A closing note: these ayat in prayer

Ibn Kathir opens the surah with two reports about the Prophet ﷺ reciting it. Malik narrated that Jubayr bin Mutʿim said: "I heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting Surat at-Tur while praying Maghrib. Surely, I have never heard a more beautiful voice or recitation than his recitation" — a hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs. And al-Bukhari recorded that Umm Salamah complained of being ill to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he told her, "Perform Tawaf behind the crowd, while you are riding." She said, "So I performed Tawaf while the Messenger of Allah was praying beside the House, reciting at-Tur."

So these are ayat that were on his ﷺ tongue in the prayer at sunset, and beside the House itself. The warning was never delivered from a distance — it was recited, beautifully, by the one who believed it most.

passages.title: The righteous in gardens and bliss
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the sūrah's answer to the passage of punishment that comes before them: having described the fate of the miserable, Allah now turns and describes the destination of the happy. Ibn Kathir puts it exactly that way — Allah "described the destination of the happy ones… **in contrast to** the torment and punishment of the miserable." That contrast is what holds ayat 17–20 together as one unit. It is a single unbroken picture: first *where* the people of taqwa are (ayah 17), then *what* they are given and *what* they are spared (ayah 18), then the words spoken to them as they eat and drink (ayah 19), and finally the posture and the company in which they will live for ever (ayah 20).

## Ayah 17 — who they are, and where they are

"Indeed, the righteous will be in Gardens and bliss."

The people named here are **al-muttaqūn**. Ibn Kathir renders the phrase as "those who have Taqwa," keeping the Arabic word rather than flattening it; the translation above gives it as "the righteous." Between those two renderings you have the sense of it: these are not simply pleasant people, but people whose lives were shaped by a mindfulness of Allah.

Notice that Allah names two things, not one: **Gardens** and **bliss** — or, in Ibn Kathir's wording, "Gardens and Delight." The Gardens are the place; the delight is what fills it. A believer is not merely relocated to a beautiful address — he is placed inside an ongoing state of enjoyment.

## Ayah 18 — the gift given, and the ruin withheld

"…enjoying whatever their Lord will have granted them. And their Lord will have saved them from the torment of the Blaze."

**"Enjoying" — fākihīn.** Ibn Kathir explains this as "enjoying the various types of delight that Allah has granted them therein, such as various types of foods, drinks, clothes, dwelling places, mounts, and so forth." That list is worth pausing over. It is deliberately ordinary — the same categories that make up a comfortable human life in this world: what you eat, what you drink, what you wear, where you live, what carries you. Paradise is not described in abstractions the heart cannot grip. It is described in the currency of things we already know we want, so that the longing is real and not merely theoretical.

**Two blessings, not one.** The ayah is built out of two halves, and each half turns on the same phrase: *their Lord.* Their Lord *gave* them; their Lord *saved* them. This is the shape of complete safety: every good thing handed over, and every dreadful thing kept away. Ibn Kathir draws attention precisely to the second half — "He saved them from the torment of the Fire, **which is a bounty itself**." That is a point easy to skim past. We normally count our blessings as things we received. Here the Qur'an counts as a blessing something that did *not* happen to us. Rescue is a gift, even before reward is a gift.

**And then, on top of all that.** Ibn Kathir adds: "Added to this blessing is the fact that they were entered into Paradise, which has delights that no eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard, nor has a heart ever imagined." So the accounting runs in three stages: saved from the Fire, then admitted to the Garden, then given inside it what the human imagination has no equipment to picture. The listed comforts — food, drink, clothing, homes, mounts — are the part we can be told about. Beyond them lies a whole order of delight for which no description exists, because description works by comparison and there is nothing here to compare it to.

## Ayah 19 — "because of what you used to do"

"[They will be told,] 'Eat and drink happily for what you used to do.'"

Now a voice speaks to them. Up to this point Allah has been describing them from outside; here they are addressed directly, in the middle of their enjoyment, and what they are told is simply: *eat and drink*.

**Hanī'an.** The word rendered "happily" here — and rendered "at ease" in the companion verse Ibn Kathir cites — is the note the whole ayah is tuned to. Earthly eating and drinking is rarely fully at ease: there is the worry of what it cost, whether it is lawful, what follows it, whether it will be taken away. This is consumption with none of that residue.

**"For what you used to do."** Ibn Kathir links this to Allah's words elsewhere: *"Eat and drink at ease for that which you have sent on before you in days past!"* (69:24) — and glosses the meaning as "this is the just reward for your deeds." The Garden is placed in relation to a life already lived; what was sent ahead is what is met on arrival.

**But do not misread it as a wage.** Ibn Kathir immediately guards the point: "this is the just reward for your deeds; **surely, all this is a favour from Allah and a reward from Him**." Both statements are true at once, and mainstream Sunni belief holds them together rather than letting either swallow the other. Deeds genuinely matter — the ayah says so plainly, and it would be a distortion of the verse to pretend otherwise. And yet the whole thing is named a favour from Allah. So the believer works as though the reward depends on his effort, and hopes as one who knows it is a gift.

## Ayah 20 — thrones in rows, and the company of the Garden

"They will be reclining on thrones, [neatly] lined up [facing one another]; and We will pair them with maidens with wide, lovely eyes."

**Reclining.** Ibn Kathir's rendering fills the word out: "They will recline **(with ease)** on thrones." Reclining is the posture of someone with nowhere to be and nothing to fear — not the posture of a servant on duty, but of an honoured guest whose work is finished. The passage leaves its subject at rest.

**Thrones lined up — surur maṣfūfah.** Ibn Kathir preserves an early explanation here with its chain of transmission: Ath-Thawrī reported from Ḥusayn, from Mujāhid, from **Ibn ʿAbbās** — "Thrones in howdahs." As for *maṣfūfah* — "lined up," "arranged in rows" — Ibn Kathir explains that it means "they will be facing each other," and supports this from the Qur'an itself: *"Facing one another on thrones"* (37:44).

That single word carries more than furniture arrangement. The seating of Paradise is *social*. Nobody is turned away from anybody; nobody sits behind anybody. There are no backs of heads, no bad seats, no far table. Whatever grudges, ranks, exclusions and awkwardnesses shaped how people sat together in this world, in that gathering everyone is placed face to face. The bliss of ayah 17 turns out to include company.

**"We will pair them."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief and restrained: "We made for them righteous spouses, beautiful wives from al-Ḥūr al-ʿAyn." He then declines to say more, noting that he has described al-Ḥūr al-ʿAyn in several other places in his Tafsir and so does not need to repeat it here — and it is worth following that restraint. The Qur'an gives us enough to long for the Garden and not enough to fantasise about it in detail. Notice too the language Ibn Kathir uses: *marriage*, *spouses* — a bond and a companionship, not merely a possession.

## Living it

**Count what did not happen to you.** Ayah 18 teaches the believer to read his own life the way Ibn Kathir reads this verse: being saved from the Fire *is itself a bounty*. The sins you were kept from, the calamities that passed you by, the ignorance you were pulled out of — these belong on the ledger of blessings just as much as what you were handed.

**Let the two halves of ayah 18 shape your duʿā'.** "Their Lord granted them… their Lord saved them." Ask for both: the giving and the guarding. A believer who asks only for good things has asked for half.

**Long for what you cannot picture.** Ibn Kathir names foods, drinks, clothes, homes and mounts — and then says there is more in Paradise than any eye has seen or any heart has imagined. Let the concrete list start the longing, and let the unimaginable remainder keep it from ever growing small.

**Hope without arrogance, work without despair.** Ayah 19 says the Garden is "for what you used to do," and Ibn Kathir says all of it is "a favour from Allah and a reward from Him." Hold both. Work as one whose deeds count — and enter, if Allah wills, knowing Who gave it.

passages.title: Families reunited and Paradise conversation
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat show us the people of Paradise not alone but together — first reunited with the family they loved, then given the food, drink and service of Paradise, and finally turning to one another to talk about the life they left behind. What holds the passage together is that one word: *together*. Ayah 21 gathers the family, ayat 22–24 furnish the gathering, and ayat 25–28 let us overhear what they say to each other once they are safe.

## Ayah 21: the family is put back together

Allah says that those who believed, and whose offspring followed them in faith, will have their offspring joined to them — and nothing of their deeds will be decreased.

Ibn Kathir opens his comment by saying this ayah affirms Allah's favour, generosity, graciousness, compassion and beneficence towards His creation. The situation it addresses is one every believing parent can picture: parents who reached a high rank, and children who believed but, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "did not perform deeds as goodly as their parents." In Paradise, ranks are real and they differ. So would a family be split up by the very ranking that rewards them?

No. Ibn Kathir explains that when the offspring of righteous believers imitate their parents regarding faith, Allah elevates them to their parents' ranks even though their own deeds did not match — and **Allah will comfort the eyes of the parents by seeing their offspring elevated to their grades**. Ibn Kathir adds that Allah will gather them together in the best manner, and will not decrease the reward or the grades of those higher in rank for joining them together.

That same point comes from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Verily, Allah elevates the ranks of the believers' offspring to rank of their parents, even though the latter have not performed as well as the former, so that the eyes of the parents are comforted" — and then recited this ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded this statement from Sufyan Ath-Thawri from Ibn 'Abbas. In another report Ibn Abi Hatim records Ibn 'Abbas defining who is meant: "They are the offspring of the believers who died on the faith. If the ranks of their parents are higher than their ranks, they will be joined with their parents."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same wording as a statement of the Prophet ﷺ reported by Ibn 'Abbas — that Allah elevates the ranks of the believers' children to the rank of their parents, even though the children do not deserve the same rank as their parents deserve, so that the eyes of the parents are comforted. Maʿārif traces it to Hakim, al-Baihaqi in his *Sunan*, al-Bazzar, Abu Nuʿaim in *al-Hilyah*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, as quoted by Mazhari.

**The reunion runs in both directions.** Maʿārif also brings a narration recorded in Tabarani, in which Saʿid ibn Jubayr reports from Ibn 'Abbas — and, the narrator says, he thinks Ibn 'Abbas reported it from the Prophet ﷺ: when a person enters Paradise he will inquire about his parents, his wife and his children, and will be told that they have not attained his grade. He will say, "O Lord! I had worked not only for myself, but for all of them." And Allah will command that they all be kept together with him in the same rank of Paradise. So it is not only children lifted to parents; it is a whole household drawn up to whoever among them stood highest.

## The phrases of the ayah

**"To them shall We join their offspring."** Notice who does the joining. It is not something the family arranges among themselves or earns; Ibn Kathir's comment is that *Allah* will gather them together in the best manner. It is done *to* them.

**"Whose offspring follow them in faith."** Faith is the condition the ayah names. Ibn Kathir is explicit that the children's deeds were not as good as their parents', and Ibn 'Abbas describes them as "the offspring of the believers who died on the faith." What qualifies a child for that reunion is belief, not a matching record of works.

**"And We shall not decrease the reward of their deeds in anything."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, citing Qurtubi, that *alatna* is the first person plural of *alata*, which literally means to decrease, to reduce or to diminish. This closes an objection before it is raised. If children are lifted to a rank their deeds did not qualify them for, is the difference taken out of the parents' account? No — Maʿārif says plainly that no part of the reward of the parents will be diminished to make up for the children's deeds; this equalisation takes place as a result of Allah's grace. Ibn 'Abbas said the same: "No part of the reward their parents received for their good deeds will be reduced for them."

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir gathers several narrations here.

Abdullah, son of Imam Ahmad, recorded that 'Ali said that Khadijah asked the Prophet ﷺ about two of her children who died during the time of Jahiliyyah, and he ﷺ said, "They are both in the Fire." When he saw sadness on her face, he said, "If you saw their dwelling place, you would hate them." She said, "O Allah's Messenger! What about my children with you?" He said, "They are in Paradise." Then he ﷺ said, "Verily, the believers and their offspring will dwell in Paradise, while the idolators and their offspring will dwell in the Hellfire" — and he recited this ayah. Ibn Kathir brings the report precisely because the Prophet ﷺ tied it to ayah 21, and its point is the ayah's point: what carries a child into that reunion is faith.

Then Ibn Kathir turns the relationship around. It is Allah's grace and favour that He grants the children this blessing because of the good deeds of their parents — and He also grants His favour to parents on account of their offspring invoking Allah for them. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Verily, Allah shall elevate the grade of a righteous servant in Paradise, who will ask, 'O Lord! How did I earn this?' Allah will reply, 'Through your son's invoking Me to forgive you.'"

Ibn Kathir is careful with this one: the hadith has an authentic chain of narration, but it was not recorded in the Sahih this way. He then supplies a witnessing narration for it from Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "When the Son of Adam dies, his record of deeds will cease except in three cases: an ongoing charity, knowledge that people are benefiting from and a righteous son who invokes Allah for him."

Read alongside ayah 21, these draw a picture of the family as a single economy of mercy. The parents' faith pulls the children up; the children's *istighfār* — their asking Allah to forgive their parents — raises the parents. And neither is diminished by the other.

## "Every person is a pledge for that which he has earned"

Immediately after this outpouring of grace, ayah 21 closes with a hard, level sentence: **كُلُّ امْرِئٍ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ** — every person is a pledge for that which he has earned.

Ibn Kathir reads the placement as deliberate. After Allah mentioned His favour of elevating the offspring to the ranks of their parents, even though the deeds of the former did not qualify them, He affirmed His fairness in that He does not punish anyone for the mistakes of others. Every person will be responsible for his actions, and no sin committed by others shall ever be added to one's load, **even if committed by his or her parents or offspring**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Ibn Kathir on exactly this point.

This is the passage's balance, and it is worth sitting with. Grace flows upward through a family and lifts people beyond what they earned; guilt does not flow at all. Ibn Kathir supports the principle with the parallel Allah cites at 74:38–41: "Every person is a pledge for what he has earned, except those on the Right. In Gardens, they will ask one another about the criminals" — a passage which, strikingly, also ends with the people of Paradise turning to one another and talking, exactly as ours will in ayah 25.

## Ayat 22–24: the hospitality

**"And We shall provide them with fruit and meat such as they desire" (ayah 22).** Ibn Kathir's gloss: various types and kinds of fruits and meat, whatever they wish for and desire. The measure of the provision is simply what they want.

**"There they shall pass from hand to hand a cup" (ayah 23).** The cup moves between them — this is a social scene, not solitary consumption. Ad-Dahhak said the cup is of wine.

Allah then names what is *absent* from it: **لَا لَغْوٌ فِيهَا وَلَا تَأْثِيمٌ** — free from any *laghw* and free from *taʼthīm*. Ibn Kathir explains that when they drink, they do not say any idle, vain words or utter dirty, sinful speech like the drunken people in this life do. Ibn 'Abbas said *laghw* means falsehood and *taʼthīm* means lying. Mujahid said, "They do not curse each other nor sin." Qatadah put his finger on why: "These were the consequences of drinking in this life, and Shaytan helped in this regard. Allah purified the wine of the Hereafter from the ills and harm caused by the wine of this life."

So the drink of Paradise is stripped of everything that makes drink destructive here — Ibn Kathir names headaches, stomachaches and intoxication, citing the parallels "White, delicious to the drinkers. Neither will they have *ghawl* from that nor will they suffer intoxication therefrom" (37:46–47) and "Wherefrom they will get neither any aching of the head nor any intoxication" (56:19). Notice how much of the negation concerns *speech*. Ibn Kathir stresses that this wine will not cause those who drink it to utter false, vain words that carry no benefit, full of foolishness and evil. What is guarded in Paradise is not only the body but the company: no gathering there will curdle. That matters enormously in a passage whose whole subject is being reunited with the people you love.

**"And there will go round boy-servants of theirs, to serve them as if they were preserved pearls" (ayah 24).** Ibn Kathir says this is a description of the servants and aides the believers will have in Paradise: beautiful, graceful in appearance, clean and neat as well-preserved pearls. He cites alongside it, "Immortal boys will go around them with cups, and jugs, and a glass of flowing wine" (56:17–18).

## Ayat 25–28: the conversation

**"And some of them draw near to others, questioning" (ayah 25).** Ibn Kathir's comment is quietly beautiful: the believers will draw near to each other talking and remembering their actions and conditions in this life, just as people in this life talk while drinking, especially when they become intoxicated. The comparison is drawn and then transformed: the same warmth of conversation, but everything ugly that attends it here has already been removed in ayah 23.

And what do they talk about? Not the fruit, not the servants, not their ranks. They talk about **fear**.

**"Aforetime, we were afraid in the midst of our families" (ayah 26).** Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "in the life of world and in the midst of our families, we were afraid of our Lord and fearful of His torment and punishment." Note where the fear was located — in the midst of their families, surrounded by the very people ayah 21 has just restored to them. That is where the trembling was kept.

**"So Allah has been gracious to us, and has saved us from the torment of the *samūm*" (ayah 27).** Ibn Kathir: "He has granted us a favour and saved us from what we feared." The shape of the sentence is worth noticing. They do not say "so we escaped," or "so our deeds saved us." They attribute the whole outcome to Allah's kindness. The punishment they were spared, *ʿadhāb al-samūm*, Ibn Kathir renders simply as the torment of the Fire.

**"Verily, we used to invoke Him before" (ayah 28).** The one thing they name from their old lives is calling on Allah. Ibn Kathir explains: "we used to invoke Him with submission and humility, and He accepted our invocation and gave us what we wished." Set this beside the narration about the son asking forgiveness for his father, and beside ayah 21, and one thread runs through the whole passage: calling on Allah is what quietly builds families in Paradise — the parent's supplication, the child's supplication, the frightened prayer whispered at home.

**"Verily, He is al-Barr, ar-Rahīm"** — rendered in this commentary as "the Most Subtle, the Most Merciful." The passage ends where it had to: with two of the names Allah gives Himself. The people of Paradise, having been given family, food, drink, service and safety, do not praise the gifts. They praise the Giver.

## Living it

- **Faith is the family tie that lasts.** Ayah 21 makes *following in faith* the condition of reunion. Whatever else a parent transmits, this is the inheritance that reaches the next world.
- **Pray for your parents, living or dead.** The narration Imam Ahmad recorded says plainly that a servant's grade in Paradise is elevated through his son's invoking Allah to forgive him — and the hadith in Sahih Muslim names a righteous son who invokes Allah for his parent as one of only three things that outlive us.
- **Do not fear that your family will cost you.** Nothing is deducted from the parents' reward when Allah lifts their children to them; Maʿārif is explicit that this happens as a result of Allah's grace. Grace is not a fixed pool being divided.
- **And do not lean on your family either.** *Every person is a pledge for that which he has earned.* No one else's record will carry you, and no one else's sins will be added to your load.
- **Keep the fear of ayah 26 where it belongs — at home.** The people who end up in that conversation were people who feared their Lord in the midst of their families, and who kept calling on Him. Ayat 27 and 28 are simply what that fear turned into.

passages.title: Not a soothsayer, a madman, or a poet
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Allah's own defence of His Messenger ﷺ. Having commanded him in ayah 29 to keep on reminding people, Allah then takes up, one by one, the labels the Quraysh threw at him — soothsayer, madman, poet, forger — and refutes each of them, closing in ayah 34 with a challenge that will never be met. Ibn Kathir titles the whole section exactly this way: "Absolving the Prophet ﷺ of the False Accusations the Idolators made against Him." What holds the six ayat together is a single courtroom-like movement: a command to carry on preaching, a clearing of the Prophet's ﷺ name, and then the burden of proof turned back onto the accusers.

## "So remind" — the command that frames everything

Ibn Kathir explains that in ayah 29 Allah "commands His Messenger ﷺ to convey His Message to His servants and remind them of His revelation that has been sent down to him." Then, he says, "Allah refutes the false accusations that the liars and sinners accused the Prophet ﷺ of."

Notice the order. The instruction to keep reminding comes *first*; the refutation of the slanders comes after it. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to pause his mission until his reputation is cleared. He is told to carry on, and Allah Himself handles the defence.

The clearing itself is placed inside a beautiful parenthesis: **"by the grace of your Lord"** (*bi-niʿmati rabbika*). The denial is not merely "you are not a soothsayer"; it is "by the grace of your Lord, you are not." What the enemies call a defect, Allah names a favour He has bestowed. And He says *your Lord* — the One who nurtures and cares for you — in the middle of a moment when the Prophet ﷺ was being publicly insulted.

## The four labels, and what each one was really claiming

Read together, the accusations are an attempt to find *any* source for the Qur'an other than Allah.

**Soothsayer (*kāhin*), ayah 29.** Ibn Kathir first states the denial plainly: "by the grace of Allah, you, O Muhammad, are not a Kahin, as the ignorant Quraysh idolators claim." Then he defines the term precisely: "A Kahin is the soothsayer who receives information from the Jinns that the Jinns are able to eavesdrop on news from heaven." So the charge is not that his words are empty. It concedes that he brings news from beyond ordinary human reach; it only disputes the channel, claiming it runs through jinn who snatch fragments of talk from the heavens.

**Madman (*majnūn*), ayah 29.** Ibn Kathir glosses this as one "whom Shaytan has possessed with insanity." Again the claim is not that his speech is ordinary, but that a hidden being stands behind it — this time deranging him rather than informing him.

**Poet (*shāʿir*), ayah 30.** Here they place what he brings in the category of poetry — a human craft. Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah as Allah "chastising the pagans for uttering false statements about the Prophet ﷺ."

**Forger, ayah 33.** In *am yaqūlūna taqawwalahu* — "Or do they say: 'He has forged it?'" — Ibn Kathir renders their claim as: "he has forged this Qur'an and brought it from his own." This is the boldest option of all: no jinn, no poetic gift, simply invention.

Four labels; the one source they refuse to name is Allah. And the little particle *am* — "or…" — heads ayah after ayah: "**Or** do they say: 'A poet!'" (30), "**Or** do their minds command them this… **or** are they people transgressing all bounds?" (32), "**Or** do they say: 'He has forged it?'" (33). The passage reads exactly like what it is — a list of alternatives being canvassed and struck out one after another, until nothing is left standing.

## "We await for him some calamity by time" — the strategy behind the sneer

Ayah 30 records not just an insult but a plan. Ibn Kathir explains what they meant: "We await a disaster to strike him, for example, death. We will be patient with him until death comes to him and we, thus, get rid of his bother and from his Message."

That is a chillingly practical calculation. They did not need to refute him. They only needed to outlive him.

Ibn Kathir preserves the moment this thinking was voiced. He reports it through Muhammad bin Isḥāq, from ʿAbdullāh bin Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When the Quraysh gathered in the Dar An-Nadwah (their meeting place) to discuss the matter of the Prophet, one of them said, 'Jail him in chains. Then we will wait and in time, a calamity will strike him; he will die just as the poets before him died, such as Zuhayr and An-Nabighah, for he is a poet just like them.'" And ayah 30, Ibn ʿAbbās adds, came down "in response to their statement."

Two poets are named, Zuhayr and an-Nābighah — men who had died. That was the whole of the argument: he is a poet like them, so he will end as they ended. It is worth sitting with how small a strategy this is. Their answer to the message was not a reply to it, but a wait for the messenger's death.

## "Say: Wait — I am waiting with you" (ayah 31)

The reply is one short sentence, and its force is in its economy. They said *natarabbaṣu* — "we await." He is told to answer with the same word back: *tarabbaṣū fa-innī maʿakum min al-mutarabbiṣīn* — "Wait! I am with you among those who wait!" The very verb of their scheming is handed straight back to them.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the meaning: "wait and I too will wait with you, and you will come to know to whom the good end and triumph shall be granted in this life and the Hereafter."

There is no argument here, no defence, no plea. Just an invitation to let time settle it — because the one who knows how the story ends can afford to say "let us both wait." Their waiting was a gamble; his was certainty. And note that Ibn Kathir specifies the good end and triumph **in this life and the Hereafter** — not only at the Resurrection. Vindication delayed is not vindication denied.

## "Or do their minds command them this?" (ayah 32)

Ayah 32 turns from the accusations to the accusers. *Am taʾmuruhum aḥlāmuhum bi-hādhā* — "Or do their minds command them this?" Ibn Kathir paraphrases: "do their minds command them to tell these lies against you (O Muhammad), **even though they know in their hearts that they are untrue and false**."

That last clause is the heart of the passage. The Qur'an is not treating these charges as an honest mistake by confused people. The word *aḥlām* refers to their reasoning faculties, and the question is aimed straight at them: is this genuinely what your minds told you to say — when your own hearts know it is false?

So the ayah offers the remaining explanation: *am hum qawmun ṭāghūn* — "or are they people transgressing all bounds?" Ibn Kathir: "surely, they are misguided, stubborn and unjust people, and this is why they say what they say about you (O Muhammad)."

This is a diagnosis worth carrying. On Ibn Kathir's reading the problem was never a shortage of evidence. It was *ṭughyān* — going past every limit, refusing to be ruled by anything. That is why ayah 33 answers "He has forged it?" not with a proof but with **"Nay! They believe not"**, which Ibn Kathir explains as: "their disbelief drives them to utter these statements." Most people assume disbelief follows from objections. Here the Qur'an reverses it: the objections follow from the disbelief. The refusal came first; the statements came out of it.

## The challenge (ayah 34)

Then comes the closing move — devastating precisely because it is so simple: *fal-yaʾtū bi-ḥadīthin mithlihi in kānū ṣādiqīn* — "Let them then produce a recitation like unto it if they are truthful."

Ibn Kathir spells out the logic: "if they are truthful in their statement that Muhammad ﷺ has forged this Qur'an and brought it of his own, then let them produce something similar to what he has brought forth, as in this Qur'an!"

The elegance is in the conditional. Their own accusation supplies the terms of the test. If a man produced this from himself, then it is a human product — and other people should be able to produce its like. The charge is allowed to stand just long enough for its own consequence to destroy it. And the phrase *in kānū ṣādiqīn*, "if they are truthful," quietly turns the question of honesty back on the accusers: someone here is not telling the truth, and the test will show who.

Ibn Kathir then widens the frame as far as it will go: "even if they combine their strength to that of the people of the earth, Jinns and mankind alike, they will never produce something like the Qur'an, or ten Surahs like it, or even one Surah!" Not only these accusers, then, and not only at three magnitudes — the whole of it, ten sūrahs, a single sūrah — but everyone, jinn and human together, at every magnitude, and never.

## Living with this passage

**Allah defends His own.** The Prophet ﷺ was called a soothsayer and a man possessed, by the Quraysh idolators around him. He was not told to answer. He was told to keep reminding, and Ibn Kathir's framing of the whole passage is that Allah then took up the refutation Himself. When a person is slandered for standing on the truth, this passage teaches where the defence properly comes from — and, from ayah 31, that the good end is settled "in this life and the Hereafter," so a delay in vindication is not an absence of it.

**Watch for reasons that arrive after the refusal.** "Nay! They believe not" (ayah 33), as Ibn Kathir reads it, describes hearts whose "disbelief drives them to utter these statements" — and minds that, per ayah 32, "know in their hearts that they are untrue and false." That is a mirror as much as a history lesson: before defending a position, it is worth asking honestly whether the reasons truly came first, or were fetched afterwards to justify a refusal already made.

**The Qur'an is still standing in the dock.** The challenge of ayah 34 was not answered by the accusers, and Ibn Kathir's comment — that mankind and jinn combined could not bring even one sūrah like it — means the evidence for this Book's origin is not locked away in the seventh century. It is in your hands, still unmatched, still asking.

passages.title: Questions their unbelief cannot answer
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** These nine ayat are a chain of questions put to the idolaters — questions that sound almost conversational, but which, taken one after another, close every door a person might escape through. Ibn Kathir titles the section "Affirming Tawhid and annulling the Plots of the Idolators," and says of it: *this is the position where Tawhid of Allah's Lordship and Divinity are affirmed.*

What holds the nine together is a single repeated word. Each of ayat 35 through 43 opens with **أَمْ** (*am*) — "or…?" The effect in Arabic is relentless: *or… or… or… or…* One by one, the possible bases a person might have for rejecting the Messenger ﷺ are named and held up empty. None of the questions is answered, because none of them can be. The silence after each one *is* the argument.

And the questions are not scattered. They move. They begin with the questioner's own existence, widen to the universe, then ask what he owns, what he has heard, what he has claimed, what he knows — and when nothing is left, they name the only motive still standing. Follow that movement and the passage reads as one closing argument rather than nine separate jabs.

## The man whose heart nearly flew away

Before the meanings, the sources give us a scene — and it is the single most illuminating thing about this passage.

Al-Bukhari recorded that **Jubayr bin Mut'im** said: "I heard the Prophet ﷺ recite Sūrat aṭ-Ṭūr in the Maghrib prayer, and when he reached this ayah — *Or were they created by nothing? Or were they themselves the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Nay, but they have no firm belief. Or are with them the treasures of your Lord? Or are they the tyrants with the authority to do as they like?* — **I felt my heart would fly away.**" Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith is collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs through various chains of narration.

Now hold on to who this man was at that moment. Ibn Kathir explains: Jubayr bin Mut'im had gone to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ **after the battle of Badr, to ransom the captured idolaters** — and **at that time he was still an idolater himself**. He was there on a negotiator's errand, and he happened to hear these very ayat recited in prayer. Hearing them, Ibn Kathir says, was one of the reasons he later embraced Islam.

So the first witness to the force of this passage is a man who was on the receiving end of it. He did not produce a rebuttal. He had the sensation of his heart trying to leave his chest. That tells you what these questions are for. They are not debating points to be scored; they are meant to be *felt* as inescapable.

## First: where did you come from? (35–36)

**أَمْ خُلِقُوا مِنْ غَيْرِ شَيْءٍ أَمْ هُمُ الْخَالِقُونَ** — "Or were they created by nothing? Or were they themselves the creators?"

Ibn Kathir puts the challenge in one sentence: Allah asks them, **were they created without a maker, or did they create themselves?** And he answers for them in two words: **Neither is true.** What remains is what he states next: **Allah is the One Who created them and brought them into existence after they were nothing.**

Notice how the ayah handles it. It does not build a case. It lays out the alternatives and lets you see which ones are left standing — the first phrasing passive (*they were created*), the second active (*they are the creators*), and neither one survivable.

Then the same question widens from the self to everything:

**أَمْ خَلَقُوا السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ ۚ بَل لَّا يُوقِنُونَ** — "Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Nay, but they have no firm belief."

Ibn Kathir says Allah is censuring the idolaters for their idolatry while asking them whether *they* created the heavens and the earth. And then he makes the observation that unlocks the whole passage: **they knew that Allah alone is the Creator, without partners with Him.** Their problem was never ignorance of that fact. Ibn Kathir states the real cause: **they fell into idolatry because they had no firm belief.**

That is the diagnosis the rest of the questions are written against. These are not people who had never heard that Allah made the sky. They are people in whom that knowledge had not become firm belief — and so it governed nothing. Every question that follows is aimed at a man who already knows the answer.

## Second: so what exactly do you own, and what have you heard? (37–38)

If Allah alone is Creator, the next question is what these objectors imagine is in their own hands.

**أَمْ عِندَهُمْ خَزَائِنُ رَبِّكَ أَمْ هُمُ الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ** — "Or are with them the treasures of your Lord? Or are they the tyrants with the authority to do as they like?"

Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves: **do they have the authority to do whatever they will in His kingdom? Do they hold the keys to His treasures in their hands?** And of *al-muṣayṭirūn* — rendered here "the tyrants with the authority to do as they like" — he asks: **are they the tyrants who would hold the creation to account?** Then he shuts the door: **Never. Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored, is the only King and Owner of existence, and He does what He wills.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani) supplies the very human argument this was answering. This ayah, he explains, responds to **one of the objections the disbelievers of Makkah raised frequently against the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ**: they used to ask why *he* was chosen for messengership, and not one of the outstanding chiefs of the tribe. The answer the ayah gives, Usmani says, is that **the selection of prophets is the exclusive prerogative of Allah. He has the treasures of knowledge, and it is He who decides to whom they should be given.** Then Usmani names what is buried inside their complaint: their attitude in objecting to His decision **is tantamount to claiming that the disposal of these treasures should have been in their hands, and that they should have the decisive power to select prophets.**

That is the sting. "It should have been someone else" is a sentence that only makes sense in the mouth of someone who owns the keys.

Reason having been closed off, one avenue is left — a private channel to the unseen:

**أَمْ لَهُمْ سُلَّمٌ يَسْتَمِعُونَ فِيهِ ۖ فَلْيَأْتِ مُسْتَمِعُهُم بِسُلْطَانٍ مُّبِينٍ** — "Or have they a stairway, by means of which they listen? Then let their listener produce some manifest proof."

Ibn Kathir: do they have a stairway to heaven — **to the place where the angels are** — by which they listen in? And then the challenge no one ever took up: **let their listener produce evidence to the truth of their actions and statements.** Ibn Kathir states the outcome flatly: **they will never be able to do so, and therefore they have nothing and have no evidence for their stance.**

Usmani reads the placement of this question exactly as the sequence suggests: their arguments against Islam having **failed on rational grounds**, the only possibility left was that they had **a direct link with Allah** by which they had ensured their faith was true — **but no one could bring any proof of having such a link.** Reason was closed in 35–37; revelation is closed here. The stairway is not there.

## Third: then look at what you have actually claimed (39–41)

With nothing owned and nothing heard, the questions turn to the content of their creed — and simply describe it back to them.

**أَمْ لَهُ الْبَنَاتُ وَلَكُمُ الْبَنُونَ** — "Or has He only daughters and you have sons?"

Ibn Kathir sets out what they held: they claimed Allah has daughters and that the angels are female. Yet **the pagans chose for themselves male offspring and preferred them instead of females** — so much so that when one of them was brought the good news of a daughter being born, **his face would turn dark on account of his suppressed anger.** And then, having assigned to Allah the very children they could not bear to receive, **they made the angels Allah's daughters and worshipped them besides Allah.** Ibn Kathir says Allah sends in this ayah a strong warning, a stern admonition, and a sure promise.

The ayah does not argue. It puts their two attitudes side by side — what they wanted for themselves, what they handed to Allah — and lets the contradiction stand in the open.

**أَمْ تَسْأَلُهُمْ أَجْرًا فَهُم مِّن مَّغْرَمٍ مُّثْقَلُونَ** — "Or is it that you ask a wage from them, so that they are burdened with a load of debt?"

Here the question turns to the Messenger ﷺ himself and tests a worldly explanation for their resistance. Ibn Kathir reads *ajr* as remuneration **for preaching Allah's message to them**, and answers on his behalf: **Nay, you do not ask them for a wage.** Then *maghram* — a debt — and *muthqalūn*, weighed down under it. Ibn Kathir's note on that state is quietly perceptive: in such a situation **one will complain of the least bothersome thing and feel it difficult and burdensome for him.**

So: is some cost being extracted from them that has soured them on the message? The ayah raises the possibility and Ibn Kathir closes it. He asks them for nothing. Another door shut.

**أَمْ عِندَهُمُ الْغَيْبُ فَهُمْ يَكْتُبُونَ** — "Or that the Unseen is with them, and they write it down?"

Do they have the unseen open in front of them, transcribing it? Ibn Kathir's answer is a foundation of belief: **they do not have knowledge of the Unseen, for none in the heavens or earth knows the Unseen except Allah.**

That single sentence disqualifies the whole posture of confident denial. Whoever speaks about the unseen is either reporting what Allah revealed or making it up. There is no third source, and by Ibn Kathir's statement they have no access to the first.

## Last: nothing left but scheming — and then the door closes (42–43)

**أَمْ يُرِيدُونَ كَيْدًا ۖ فَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا هُمُ الْمَكِيدُونَ** — "Or do they intend a plot? But those who disbelieve are themselves plotted against!"

No argument, no revelation, no authority, no grievance. What is left is *kayd* — scheming. Ibn Kathir renders the question: do these people who utter such statements about the Messenger and his religion **seek to deceive the people and plot against the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions?** And then the answer: **if they do, let them know that their plots will only harm them. Therefore, they are being plotted against rather than being the plotters.**

That is the reversal the ayah itself performs. They intend to be the schemers; the word the ayah puts on them, *al-makīdūn*, is "those plotted against." The trap they are digging carries their own name.

**أَمْ لَهُمْ إِلَٰهٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ ۚ سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ** — "Or have they a god other than Allah? Glorified be Allah from all that they ascribe as partners."

The final *am* returns to where the sequence began, but now with everything else stripped away. Ibn Kathir says this ayah contains **harsh refutation directed at the idolaters for worshipping the idols and calling upon rivals along with Allah** — and then notes what Allah does next: **He glorifies His Most Honorable Self from what they ascribe to Him, their lies and their idolatry.**

Notice how the passage ends. Not with one more question, and not with a further proof. It ends with **سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ** — glory be to Allah — declaring Him far above every partner they invented. The nine questions were addressed to them. The last word is addressed to Him.

## Living it

**Certainty, not just information.** The people in this passage, Ibn Kathir says, *knew* that Allah alone is the Creator without partners — and still fell into idolatry, **because they had no firm belief**. That is a diagnosis worth turning on ourselves. The work of faith is not only to learn what is true, but to let it settle deeply enough that it actually governs what we do.

**Watch what an objection assumes.** Usmani's reading of ayah 37 concerned a specific complaint: why was *this* man chosen as Messenger, and not a chief of the tribe? His verdict on that complaint is worth sitting with — that objecting to Allah's decision here amounted to claiming the treasuries should have been in their own hands. It is a fair question to ask of our own protests about what Allah has decided and distributed.

**Ask the passage's questions of yourself.** Where did I come from (35)? Who made this world (36)? What do I actually know of the unseen (41)? These are not weapons for winning arguments. They are the questions Jubayr bin Mut'im heard in a Maghrib prayer while he was still an idolater, on an errand for the other side — and they nearly carried his heart out of his chest.

**Do not fear the schemers.** Ibn Kathir names the targets of the plotting plainly: the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions. And he names the outcome just as plainly — the plots will only harm the plotters, who are themselves the ones being plotted against. When you are the one being schemed against, that is not a slogan. It is the promise the ayah makes.

passages.title: Their obstinacy and the Day awaiting them
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat come near the close of Sūrat aṭ-Ṭūr. They describe a heart that no evidence can reach, and then tell the Prophet ﷺ what to do about it: step back, and let the Day they are heading toward do the answering. Ibn Kathir titles this section "The Stubbornness of the Idolators; Their Punishment" — and that is exactly the thread that holds the four ayat together. Ayah 44 shows the obstinacy; ayah 45 hands them over to their Day; ayah 46 removes the two things a person normally leans on when disaster comes; ayah 47 reveals that a smaller punishment is already at work on them in this world, and that they have not understood it.

## Ayah 44: the sky falls and they call it weather

"And if they were to see a piece of the heaven falling down, they would say: 'Clouds gathered in heaps!'"

Ibn Kathir explains that the falling piece is not scenery — it is punishment, descending **on them**. And still, he says, "they would not believe it is coming their way, saying that these are layers of clouds on top of each other."

Feel how devastating that picture is. Something is coming down out of the sky, and their verdict on it is a single flat word — *saḥāb*, "cloud" — which Ibn Kathir unpacks as clouds heaped and layered one on top of another. A doom is descending and they file it under ordinary weather. Not a moment of fear, not a second look. This is the mind that has already decided, so that every incoming fact is bent to fit the decision it has already made. Ibn Kathir calls it exactly that: Allah here reaffirms "the stubbornness of the idolators and their ignorance of what goes around them."

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it another ayah where Allah describes the same disposition: "And even if We opened to them a gate from the heaven and they were to keep on ascending thereto (all day long), they would surely say (in the evening): 'Our eyes have been dazzled. Nay, we are a people bewitched'" (15:14–15). Even a miracle they climbed through with their own bodies would be explained away by nightfall — first as an optical trick, then as sorcery. Put the two passages together and the message is plain: the problem was never a shortage of evidence. A sign only persuades someone willing to be persuaded.

## Ayah 45: "So leave them"

"So leave them alone till they meet their Day, in which they will sink into a fainting (with horror)."

Ibn Kathir supplies the unspoken address here: *fa-dharhum* — "So leave them alone" — is spoken to the Prophet ﷺ, "O Muhammad." Directly after describing a stubbornness that no falling sky could dent, the instruction is to stop pressing.

Notice how the ayah handles time. It does not say *leave them forever*; it says leave them **until** — until they come face to face with a day that is already theirs. The Qur'an calls it "their Day," as though it has their name on it. Ibn Kathir identifies it as the Day of Resurrection.

And what meets them there is described with one verb, rendered here as sinking into a fainting — a collapse of the senses under sheer horror. It is a pointed reversal. The whole of ayah 44 was about people who felt nothing when the sky itself was falling on them: flat, unmoved, unimpressed. On that Day the numbness ends. What they refused to feel voluntarily, they will feel involuntarily, and it will overwhelm them completely.

## Ayah 46: the two supports removed

"The Day when their plotting shall not avail them at all, nor will they be helped."

This ayah names the Day again in order to strip it bare. When trouble arrives, a person reaches for one of two things: his own cleverness, or someone else's strength. Ayah 46 closes both doors in a single breath.

*Kayd* is scheming — the planning and manoeuvring a person arranges in his own favour. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "their deceit and plots they planned in this life," and says that on the Day of Resurrection these "shall not help them in the least." Everything they contrived in this world is carried into that Day and found to be worth nothing. Not merely a little help — the ayah says it will not benefit them *whatsoever*.

Then: "nor will they be helped." The verb is passive — no rescuer arrives from outside either. A person who cannot save himself and whom no one else will save has run out of options entirely, and that is precisely the state ayah 46 describes.

## Ayah 47: a punishment that arrives earlier

"And verily, for those who do wrong, there is another punishment before this; but most of them know not."

Having placed the great reckoning in the future, the passage now turns and points at the present. Ibn Kathir explains "another punishment before this" as "the torment in this world." Before the Day arrives, there are smaller reckonings already in motion.

Ibn Kathir supports this with a parallel ayah: "And verily, We will make them taste of the near torment prior to the supreme torment (in the Hereafter), in order that they may return" (32:21). Read that closing clause carefully, because it changes the whole tone: *in order that they may return*. The smaller punishment is not the first instalment of revenge. It is a summons — a shock delivered early, while there is still time to turn back.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (Muhammad Taqi Usmani) identifies what this worldly punishment looked like for the people addressed: "the punishments faced by the disbelievers right in this world, like famines and the deterrent defeat in the battle of Badr." Concrete history, not abstraction — hunger, and a battlefield that broke their confidence.

Observe also the wording of ayah 47. It does not say "for them"; it says **"for those who do wrong."** The sentence widens from the particular deniers being described to a stated category. The rule is given by the trait, not by the name.

## "But most of them know not" — the diagnosis

The last clause of ayah 47 is the most searching line in the passage, and Ibn Kathir's comment on it is worth quoting at length. He renders the divine intent as: "We will torment them in the life of the world and test them with various hardships, so that they might go back and repent. However, they do not understand what is happening to them or why, because when the torment is removed, they revert to committing the worst of what they used to do before."

That is a portrait of a whole cycle. Hardship comes. It is a knock at the door. But they never ask who is knocking — they read the famine as bad luck and the defeat as bad tactics, exactly as in ayah 44 they read a falling sky as a cloud formation. Then the pressure lifts. And instead of the relief becoming gratitude and change, it becomes licence: they go back not merely to what they were doing, but to "the worst of what they used to do before."

So the ignorance in "most of them know not" is not a lack of information. They knew perfectly well that they were hungry and that they had been defeated. What they did not know was *what it meant* — that these were a summons from their Lord, sent, as 32:21 says, "in order that they may return." The same blindness that made a descending punishment look like weather made a chastening trial look like misfortune.

## Living it

**Read your hardships.** The most transferable lesson here is a question to ask when life goes hard: not only "how do I get out of this?" but "is my Lord calling me back with this?" The parallel Ibn Kathir cites (32:21) states the purpose openly — the lesser difficulty comes "in order that they may return." A believer who takes that seriously treats a setback as an invitation to repentance rather than a run of bad luck.

**Watch what you do when the pressure lifts.** Ibn Kathir puts his finger on the exact point of failure: not the hardship, but the aftermath. The test of whether a difficulty taught you anything is what you become when it ends. If relief returns you straight to your old habits — or worse — then the message was received and discarded.

**Do not expect evidence alone to convert anyone.** Ayah 44, with 15:14–15 beside it, should quietly cure us of the idea that one more argument, one more proof, will do it. Some hearts will call a falling sky a cloud. That knowledge protects a caller to Allah from both bitterness and burnout.

**Know when to step back.** "So leave them" in ayah 45 is a divine instruction, not a personal defeat. And it is not abandonment: the ayah itself fixes the term — leave them *until they meet their Day*. Handing a matter over to Allah is not dropping it. It is placing it where it will certainly be settled.

That is the balance these four ayat leave us holding. The obstinate are left to their Day, and nothing they schemed and no one they counted on will reach them there. Yet even now, before that Day, the smaller trials keep arriving — and Allah states plainly why He sends them: so that they may return. The door in ayah 47 is still open. Ibn Kathir's warning is simply that most people walk past it without recognising it for what it is.

passages.title: Patience, praise, and night worship
passages.tafsir:
Surah at-Tur ends not with a threat but with an instruction to its Messenger ﷺ: bear it patiently, because you are being watched over — and fill the waiting with praise. Ayah 48 gives the consolation and the command; ayah 49 spreads that command across the hours of the night and into the moments before dawn. What holds the two together is a single movement: from a heart under pressure, to a heart under Allah's care, to a tongue and body occupied with worship.

## Where these words fall

The surah has just described the hardened refusal of the idolaters. Ibn Kathir explains ayah 44 — "if they were to see a piece of the heaven falling down" as punishment coming toward them — as their refusing even then to believe it, dismissing it as "layers of clouds on top of each other," much as Allah says elsewhere that had a gate of heaven been opened for them to climb through, they would have said their eyes were dazzled and they were bewitched (15:14–15). So the Prophet ﷺ is told in ayah 45 to leave them until the Day they meet, when (ayah 46) their scheming will not help them and no one will come to their aid, and Ibn Kathir notes that ayah 47 promises the wrongdoers "another punishment before this" — torment in this world, as in "We will make them taste of the near torment prior to the supreme torment, in order that they may return" (32:21). Yet, he adds, most of them do not grasp what is happening to them or why: when the affliction lifts, they go back to the worst of what they were doing.

That is the setting. The enemy is unmoved, the reckoning is real but not yet, and the Messenger ﷺ is left standing in the gap. Ayat 48–49 tell him what to do in that gap.

## "So be patient with your Lord's decree"

**وَٱصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ** — Ibn Kathir renders it "So wait patiently for the decision of your Lord," and glosses it plainly: be patient in the face of their annoyance and do not be troubled by it. The patience commanded here is not resignation to a shapeless fate; it is patience *for a decision that is coming*. Allah has already announced in ayah 47 that a judgement is in motion. The Prophet ﷺ is being asked to hold his position until it arrives.

## "For you are truly under Our Eyes"

This is the heart of the passage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the human scene: the hostility of the enemies, their opposition and rejection, weighed on the Holy Prophet ﷺ and depressed him. So, at the very conclusion of the surah, the Qur'an says **فَإِنَّكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا** — "You are before Our Eyes," meaning, as Maʿārif puts it, *under Our care; We shall protect you from every evil, so do not be anxious about it.* It cites the parallel promise elsewhere in the Qur'an: **وَٱللَّهُ يَعْصِمُكَ مِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ** — "And Allah shall protect you from the people."

Ibn Kathir reads it the same way: "you are under Our Eyes and Protection, and We will surely protect you from the people."
