Feel the emotional logic of the sentence: *be patient — because you are in view.* That is exactly why Maʿārif can finish the thought with "do not be anxious about it." The one who is seen, cared for and protected by Allah has a reason not to panic, however loud the opposition becomes.

## "And glorify your Lord with praise"

**وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ** — *tasbīḥ* means to proclaim Allah's purity, to declare Him far above every defect and every false thing said about Him; *ḥamd* is praise. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "And proclaim the purity of your Lord along with His praise when you stand" — the two motions of a believing heart in one breath.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this is the answer to the surah's pressure: "To proclaim the purity and praise of Allah is the real purpose of life, and also the real cure of every calamity." That is a striking claim, and it explains the shape of the passage. The remedy handed to a grieving Messenger ﷺ is not a strategy against his opponents. It is worship.

## "When you stand" — three readings, all of them practice

The phrase **حِينَ تَقُومُ**, "when you stand / when you get up," is open, and the early authorities read it in more than one way. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes plainly that "'When you stand' could mean to stand up for the Salah or to arise or get up from sleep or bed." Ibn Kathir reports the readings without discarding any:

**1. When you stand for prayer.** Ad-Daḥḥāk said it means to stand for the Salah and say: "Glorious are You and with Your praise, hallowed be Your Name, exalted be Your majesty, and there is none worthy of worship except You." Ibn Kathir notes that in his *Sahih*, Muslim recorded that ʿUmar used to recite this supplication when he began the Salah, and that Ahmad and the Sunan compilers recorded it from Abu Saʿid and other Companions, who stated that the Prophet ﷺ used to say it.

**2. When you get up from sleep.** Abu al-Jawzāʾ said it means "from your sleep, from your bed," and Ibn Kathir notes that this is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir — the same preference Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records. Supporting it is the report Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: whoever gets up at night and says *"There is none worthy of worship but Allah alone, with no partner; His is the dominion and His is all praise, and He has power over all things. Glory be to Allah, and all praise is due to Allah, and there is none worthy of worship but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest; there is neither might nor power except with Allah,"* then says "My Lord, forgive me" — or supplicates — he will be responded to; and if he intends and performs ablution and prays, his prayer will be accepted. Ibn Kathir adds that al-Bukhari and the Sunan compilers also recorded this hadith.

Look at what that hadith does to a broken night's sleep. The moment of waking at some dark hour — usually wasted or resented — becomes a moment when a supplication is answered and a prayer is accepted.

**3. When you get up from a gathering.** Ibn Abī Najīḥ reported that Mujāhid explained the ayah as "from every gathering you sit in," and Abu al-Aḥwaṣ said: when a person wants to stand up from a gathering, he says *"Glory be to You, O Allah, and with Your praise."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the words of ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ on this ayah: "When you stand from a gathering, proclaim the purity and praise of Allah. If you have done any good work, your good work will be increased and enhanced. If you had done any bad deed, these words of proclamation will serve as an expiation and atonement."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this practice **kaffārat al-majlis** — the expiation of the gathering, a recitation at the end of a meeting that expiates sins — and both commentaries cite the report from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: whoever sits in a gathering in which he speaks idly a great deal, and says before he stands up to leave, *"Glory be to You, O Allah, and with Your praise; I testify that there is none worthy of worship except You; I seek Your forgiveness and I repent to You,"* Allah will forgive him what he said in that gathering. Ibn Kathir notes it was recorded by at-Tirmidhi — whose wording he gives — and by an-Nasāʾī in *[ʿAmal] al-Yawm wa-l-Laylah*, that at-Tirmidhi graded it "Hasan Sahih," and that al-Hakim recorded it in his *Mustadrak* saying its chain meets the criteria of Muslim.

**How to hold the three together.** They are not rival claims about one narrow moment so much as three doorways the same word opens: rising to pray, rising from bed, rising from a sitting. Ibn Jarir preferred the second; Ad-Daḥḥāk gave the first; Mujāhid, Abu al-Aḥwaṣ and ʿAṭāʾ the third. Each is anchored in something the Prophet ﷺ taught, so the believer who takes up all three is on safe ground with any of the readings.

## Ayah 49: the night, and the last of the stars

**وَمِنَ ٱلَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ** — "And glorify Him during part of the night." Ibn Kathir explains this as remembering and worshipping Allah by reciting the Qur'an and praying at night, and connects it to Allah's words: "And in some of the night, offer Tahajjud in it as an additional prayer for you. It may be that your Lord will raise you to *Maqām Maḥmūd*" (17:79) — the praised station. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the phrase a little: proclaiming the purity of the Lord "in parts of night" includes the Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ prayers, as well as the general *tasbīḥāt* — the words of glorification said at those hours.

Note the small word **مِنَ**, "*part* of the night." Not the whole of it. The command measures itself to a human being who must also sleep.

**وَإِدْبَارَ ٱلنُّجُومِ** — "and at the fading of the stars." The phrase marks the last of the darkness, when the stars are about to set. Ibn Kathir says this refers to the two voluntary rakʿahs before the Dawn prayer, according to a hadith from Ibn ʿAbbās, and observes that these two rakʿahs are an established Sunnah performed before the stars are about to set. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same, taking the phrase as referring to the Fajr prayer and the *tasbīḥāt* recited at that time.

The two small rakʿahs before Fajr are easy to dismiss as a formality. The Sunnah says otherwise. It is confirmed in the Two Sahihs from ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Prophet ﷺ "was never more regular and particular in offering any voluntary prayer than the two rakʿahs of the Fajr prayer," and in a narration collected by Muslim the Prophet ﷺ said: **"Two rakʿahs before Fajr are better than this life and all that is in it."**

## Living it

Read together, ayat 48–49 hand the believer a rhythm rather than a mood:

- **When the opposition bites, hold your position.** The decree is coming; the task in the meantime is patience, not panic (ayah 48).
- **Remember who is watching.** "You are truly under Our Eyes" is the reason patience is reasonable — under Allah's care and protection, as both commentaries gloss it.
- **Answer pressure with praise.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's line is worth memorising: proclaiming Allah's purity and praise is both the real purpose of life and the real cure of every calamity.
- **Take every "standing" as a cue.** Standing to pray — the opening glorification. Waking in the night — the words ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit reported, then ablution (*wuḍūʾ*, the ritual washing before prayer) and prayer if you can rise. Standing from a gathering — the words that wipe away what was idly said in it.
- **Give the night a portion** (ayah 49): Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, Qur'an, night prayer.
- **Do not skip the two rakʿahs before Fajr** — better, we are told, than this life and all that is in it.

And so the surah that closed in on a stubborn people ends by turning the reader toward the quietest acts available to anyone: a word of praise on rising, a portion of the night, two short rakʿahs while the stars go out. Ibn Kathir ends his commentary on Surat at-Tur exactly there — "all praise and gratitude is due to Allah" — which is itself the ayah being obeyed.
